content: Achiote, scientifically known as Bixa orellana, is a shrub or small tree native to the tropical regions of the American continent. The name achiote originates from the Nahuatl word achiotl, and it is also referred to as aplopas or by its original Tupi name, urucu. This plant is cultivated in its native regions as well as in Southeast Asia, where it was introduced by the Spanish during the 17th century. The plant is most recognized as the source of the natural pigment annatto, which is derived from its fruit. Achiote produces pink flowers and bright red, spiny fruits that contain red seeds. As the fruits mature, they dry and harden into brown capsules. Although the fruit itself is inedible, the seeds are harvested for their annatto content, also known as bixin. Annatto can be extracted by stirring the seeds in water. It is widely used as a natural coloring agent in food products such as cheeses, fish, and salad oils. Additionally, it serves as a key ingredient in the Mexican spice mixture recado rojo, commonly referred to as achiote paste. The seeds are ground and used as a nearly flavorless but vibrant additive in Latin American, Jamaican, and Filipino cuisines. Annatto is gaining popularity as a natural alternative to synthetic food coloring agents. Ethnomedical Uses Achiote has been traditionally used by American Indians to create body paint, particularly for the lips, which is the origin of its nickname, lipstick tree. Various parts of the plant are utilized in the preparation of medicinal remedies for conditions such as sunstroke, tonsillitis, burns, leprosy, pleurisy, apnea, rectal discomfort, and headaches. The sap extracted from the fruits is also employed in the treatment of type II diabetes and fungal infections.
